ai.definition: Algorithmic Dispute Resolution (ADR) is an application of Artificial Intelligence, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), to facilitate the resolution of disputes by suggesting fair settlements based on a database of legal precedents and evidence.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves inputting case details and evidence into an LLM. The AI analyzes these inputs against historical legal cases to suggest a settlement that is likely to be fair and legally sound, thus streamlining the dispute resolution process.
ai.problemSolved: Rapid resolution of small-claims disputes, reducing costs and time for both parties compared to traditional court proceedings or arbitration.
ai.buildProcess: Development involves training an LLM on a vast dataset of legal precedents, case law, and evidence submissions. The system is then fine-tuned using specific dispute scenarios to improve accuracy and relevance.
ai.costDrivers: Data labeling for the initial training phase; ongoing maintenance costs for software updates and improvements in AI models.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Growth potential as legal systems seek more efficient means of resolving disputes, particularly in small-claims cases.
ai.regulation: Current framework is limited; specific regulations will likely develop as the technology gains wider adoption and integration into legal processes.
ai.risks: Bias in AI models if not properly trained on diverse datasets; potential for misuse or misunderstanding by non-expert users.
ai.profitability: Potential high profitability due to cost savings for parties involved, but requires significant investment in development and validation.
ai.futureDevelopment: Improvements in AI accuracy and user interfaces, integration with blockchain for enhanced transparency and security, expansion into more complex dispute scenarios.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking processes for hardware components.

glossary.def: A technology that uses AI, particularly LLMs, to suggest fair settlements in disputes based on legal precedents and evidence.
A type of AI model designed to understand and generate human-like text across a wide range of topics and contexts.

subsystems.name: Case intake and structuring
subsystems.role: turns a plain-language complaint into a structured set of claims, facts and evidence.

subsystems.name: Legal knowledge base
subsystems.role: the grounding corpus the system reasons over, rather than inventing law.
parts: anonymised case law and tribunal decisions

subsystems.name: Retrieval layer
subsystems.role: finds the passages of law and comparable past cases relevant to the submission.

subsystems.name: Analysis and outcome model
subsystems.role: extracts the disputed facts and estimates a defensible range of outcomes.

subsystems.name: Negotiation and settlement engine
subsystems.role: lets both sides move toward agreement without revealing their limits too early.

subsystems.name: Explanation and decision layer
subsystems.role: produces a written, cited outcome a human can check and a party can appeal.

subsystems.name: Oversight, audit and integrity
subsystems.role: keeps the process lawful, logged and fair.

buildSteps.title: Pick a narrow claim type
buildSteps.detail: Start where the law is codified and disputes are high-volume and low-value — for example small unpaid invoices or undelivered goods.

buildSteps.title: Assemble a licensed, anonymised corpus
buildSteps.detail: Collect statutes, rules and past decisions for that claim type, strip personal data, and record the source and date of every document.

buildSteps.title: Define the decision taxonomy
buildSteps.detail: Set out the elements a claimant must prove, the evidence that satisfies each, the defences available, and the remedies and amounts allowed.

buildSteps.title: Build structured intake
buildSteps.detail: A guided form converts free text and uploaded documents into those elements, flagging what is missing before the case proceeds.

buildSteps.title: Ground the model in retrieval
buildSteps.detail: The language model is constrained to retrieved sources, with citations required and automatic rejection of any output not traceable to the corpus.

buildSteps.title: Back-test against past outcomes
buildSteps.detail: Run the system over closed historical cases and compare its predicted range and reasoning against what the tribunal or court actually decided.

buildSteps.title: Build the negotiation protocol
buildSteps.detail: Implement offer-and-counteroffer rules, time limits and settlement drafting, with both parties able to opt out into ordinary adjudication.

buildSteps.title: Add human review and appeal
buildSteps.detail: A registrar or adjudicator signs off decisions, and either party can escalate to a human decision-maker within a set period.

buildSteps.title: Log, monitor and pilot
buildSteps.detail: Run it as a pilot in one jurisdiction with full audit logging, then measure error rates, bias across claimant groups and user comprehension of the reasons given.

prerequisites.tech: Digitised, machine-readable case law and statutes
prerequisites.why: reasoning can only be grounded where decisions are published openly and consistently; many jurisdictions are not there yet.
plain generation is unreliable for law; retrieval plus citation is what makes answers checkable.
filing, evidence upload and video hearings must already work before AI can sit on top.
signatures, timestamps and document provenance decide whether a submission can be trusted.
questions of due process, unauthorised practice of law and enforceable automated decisions are largely unresolved.

prerequisites.tech: Auditability and explainability of model outputs
prerequisites.why: a decision that cannot be explained and reproduced cannot be appealed or reviewed.

pathway.milestone: online tribunals and e-commerce platforms handle millions of small disputes with rules-based and partly automated processes
pathway.unlocks: a working template for structured, evidence-based online resolution.

pathway.milestone: AI assistants that draft settlements and predict outcome ranges for a human adjudicator to approve
pathway.unlocks: faster case handling in small claims while a person remains accountable.

pathway.milestone: binding automated decisions for narrow, codified claim types with published reasoning
pathway.unlocks: affordable justice for amounts too small to justify conventional litigation.

pathway.milestone: cross-border recognition of automated outcomes and tiered human appeal
pathway.unlocks: portable resolution for online commerce, but only if enforceability and fairness rules converge.
